scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Original C2 independent assessment draft with ten new inference, argument or transfer questions. Content requires teacher approval.

tabs.title: Conceptual Distinctions
tabs.description: Examine the author's concepts and underlying claims.

tabs.title: Argument and Qualification
tabs.description: Evaluate how the essay limits and develops its claims.

tabs.title: Critical Transfer
tabs.description: Apply nuanced criteria to unfamiliar institutional decisions.

questions.q: What changes when resilience is treated as a moral requirement rather than a resource?
choices: Failure to recover may be blamed on a person rather than their circumstances.
Perseverance becomes a more accurate measure of intellectual ability.
Educators can distinguish effective strategies from endurance more easily.
Learners gain greater freedom to reconsider inherited goals.
questions.explanation: The opening distinguishes capacity to recover from an obligation imposed without regard to circumstances.

questions.q: Why is visible determination an unreliable sign that education is working?
choices: It is most evident among pupils whose goals are poorly chosen.
It may hide endurance under poor conditions rather than meaningful agency.
It proves that external support matters less than classroom feedback.
It gives institutions no way to observe progress over time.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph contrasts productive revision with repeated struggle caused by inadequate support.

questions.q: What does the claim about indicators 'colonising' activity chiefly criticise?
choices: The transfer of assessment practices between different subjects.
The failure to measure small changes in scores accurately.
The tendency to let measurement redefine what counts as worthwhile.
The complete absence of educational data about exploration.
questions.explanation: The metaphor describes a measure expanding beyond its original purpose and shaping judgments of value.

questions.q: Why does the writer contrast retrospective inspirational stories with advice given during hardship?
choices: Teachers can only advise students once their challenges are over.
Retrospective stories generally contain more reliable educational data.
People facing hardship are less willing to consider alternative goals.
Hindsight makes perseverance seem simpler than the ongoing constraints permit.
questions.explanation: The contrast questions how responsibly one can recommend perseverance while constraints remain unresolved.

questions.q: Which condition determines whether renewed effort has a reasonable educational purpose?
choices: Students must have already demonstrated resilience in an earlier task.
There must be a plausible prospect that effort can change the outcome.
An institution must be able to reward every display of persistence.
The revised strategy must lead to a higher score immediately.
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly distinguishes agency from endurance by asking if conditions allow meaningful change.

questions.q: Why is a score-improvement measure not simply described as false?
choices: It provides a reliable comparison of students' motivation.
It can only be valid when it includes a measure of perseverance.
It makes intellectual wandering impossible to observe.
It may accurately capture speed while missing the depth of learning.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the indicator answers a narrower question rather than necessarily reporting false data.

questions.q: A school praises pupils for overcoming repeated shortages but leaves the shortages unchanged. What is the central danger?
choices: Praise becomes a way of avoiding institutional responsibility.
Pupils will no longer wish to receive constructive criticism.
Assessment will cease to identify students who work hard.
Endurance will no longer be visible to teachers.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two warns that celebrating endurance can spare institutions from questioning persistent obstacles.

questions.q: A student abandons a narrow project to explore a more promising question. How might the author regard this?
choices: As proof that perseverance has ceased to matter educationally.
As a mistake unless the new topic leads to a better grade.
As potentially sound judgement rather than an automatic failure of grit.
As evidence that the student requires closer performance monitoring.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly treats reconsidering a poorly chosen goal as a potentially mature decision.

questions.q: Which institutional response best fits the conclusion after a learner's disappointing result?
choices: Require the learner to demonstrate greater effort before offering support.
Review both the support available and whether the assessed target remains worthwhile.
Remove assessments altogether to avoid any judgement of resilience.
Praise the learner's endurance without examining the conditions.
questions.explanation: The conclusion calls for scrutiny of constraints, metrics, choice and the legitimacy of aims.

questions.q: What would make a resilience programme more defensible by the essay's standards?
choices: Reward students who persevere longer regardless of the task.
Link every period of rest to measurable academic improvement.
Judge maturity primarily by how quickly setbacks are overcome.
Give learners resources to persist and permission to revise their goals.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph pairs the means to continue with the freedom to reconsider what matters.
